name: Charcoal mask

card.summary: A black clay or peel-off face mask containing activated charcoal, used to leave skin feeling cleaner and to lift surface oil and dirt.
card.note: Peel-off versions can tug on skin and cause irritation.

quick.overview:
A charcoal mask is a face mask made with activated charcoal, a highly porous carbon. Users apply it to the face and rinse or peel it away, aiming for clearer-looking, cleaner skin.
Activated carbon is known for adsorption, the sticking of molecules to its surface, which is why it is used in filters.[1] Cosmetic charcoal masks borrow that idea, though published clinical trials for the masks are lacking.
quick.how: The mask is spread over the face, left for the time on the label and then rinsed or peeled off. Users typically reserve it for occasional use, often on the T-zone. One 2003 T Nation forum poster mentioned using Origins' black charcoal mask as part of a skincare routine.[2]
quick.risks: Peel-off versions can pull on skin and irritate it, and any mask can cause reactions in sensitive skin. Avoid the eye area; product labels give guidance.

lead: A charcoal mask is a face mask containing activated charcoal, also called activated carbon, a highly porous form of carbon whose surface area can exceed 3,000 square metres per gram.[1] It comes as rinse-off clay masks and as peel-off gels.

Its appearance purpose is skin that looks and feels cleaner. Activated carbon works by adsorption, where molecules adhere to its surface; that property underlies its use in water and air filtration and as a poison treatment.[1]
In men's grooming discussion, a T Nation poster in 2003 listed Origins' black charcoal mask among products they liked.[2]

chain: Surface oil and debris adhere to the mask
angle.text: People use it as a weekly-style cleansing treatment to freshen skin. The charcoal is intended to bind surface impurities.

paras: Activated carbon is made by carbonising materials such as coconut husk or wood at roughly 600-900 degrees Celsius and activating them with steam or chemicals.[1]
No studies found. Research on activated carbon covers filtration and medical use, not face masks specifically.[1]

lore.intro: Charcoal masks are mentioned in older men's skincare threads.[2]

claims.claim: A charcoal mask draws out dirt and oil
claims.believers: Users say the mask leaves skin cleaner.[2]
claims.experts: Activated carbon is established as an adsorbent in filtration; no studies found test facial masks.[1]
